1:
The morning session is explained six ways and the explanations do not agree. Robertson takes it for a formal meeting after dawn to ratify what had been done illegally in the night. Clarke says the same more bluntly: proceeding against a life by night was contrary to all forms of law, so they separated for a few hours and reassembled at daybreak. Ellicott finds no pretence but a rule: sentence was not to be given at the sitting that heard the trial, so a second council was required. Calvin grants the form and denies the motive: they kept the shape of judicial proceeding so as not to be suspected of haste when they ran to the governor at an unusual hour. Wesley makes it a matter of doors, the council chamber in the temple never being opened at night. Barnes alone gives the session business to do: they had condemned him for blasphemy, which was no offence at Roman law, so the morning went in finding a civil charge Pilate could act on.

Lightfoot simply counts the breaches. Their own canon requires capital causes to be finished by day; their own canon forbids judgment on a feast day, and this was the evening of one; and the hour at which they sat was the hour appointed for the phylacteries, so that the business in hand either robbed them of their prayers or robbed their prayers of charity. Gill marks the same collision. Jerome puts it as zeal rather than law, the chief priests watching the whole night with a view to a murder.

Why the case went to Pilate at all is disputed the same way. Henry makes it necessity, the power of capital punishment having been taken from the Jews about two years before, which he reads as the sceptre departing from Judah. Barnes says they dared not stone him as they afterwards stoned Stephen, because they feared the people. Calvin answers directly: the stoning of Stephen was a tumult and proves nothing about what was permitted, and had they been free to take life they would in their fury have murdered him themselves; it was fitting instead that the Son of God be solemnly condemned by an earthly judge, that he might efface our condemnation in heaven. Chrysostom gives a motive rather than a constraint, since a secret death would have left his reputation standing. Ellicott sees a contest of jurisdictions, the ecclesiastical power seeking to make the imperial its tool and the imperial trying not to be used.

On the binding the reports differ in detail. Robertson recalls that he was bound in the garden and before Annas and may have been unbound before Caiaphas; Barnes supposes he was loosed at the trial and bound again for the move across the city. Gill offers three reasons for doing it again: security, reproach, and that the Roman judge should take him at sight for a malefactor. Origen will not let the fact pass, that they bound Jesus who looses them that are bound; and Henry turns it the same way: we who were held in the cords of our sins are loosed by his bonds as we are healed by his stripes.

Two writers stand outside the legal question. Augustine attends only to the order of the telling: the evangelist brought the night down to morning, turned back for Peter's denial, and returns now to the morning. Cyril of Jerusalem reads the journey as prophecy: the man bound and led away is the present carried to the king, and when it is objected that Pilate was no king he answers that Pilate, hearing of Galilee, sent him to Herod, who was king; and he notices that the same day made Pilate and Herod friends who had been at enmity, so that the first peace made by the peacemaker was between the men who condemned him.
3:
The word rendered repented is not the word for repentance, and everyone says so. Robertson glosses it as being sorry afterwards, a word carrying no evil sense in itself, Paul using it of his own regret over a sharp letter; what was missing was the change of life that took Peter back to Christ. Barnes puts the contrast sharpest: true repentance leads the sinner to the Saviour, this led away from the Saviour to the gallows. Calvin says Judas was not reformed but made uneasy, God opening the eyes of the reprobate far enough to feel their misery. Ellicott notices what is absent, that here there were no tears as there had been in Peter's.

What Judas had expected is guessed at rather than known. Barnes supposes he looked for a miracle of deliverance and was overwhelmed when that closed. Clarke turns the episode into evidence: had Christ been condemned on a disciple's word the charge of imposture would have stood, but the same disciple recanted, declared his Master innocent, flung back the bribe and died, clearing Christ's character by the one man positioned to destroy it.

The refusal shocks the commentators more than the treason. Chrysostom says the priests knew they had purchased a murder and were condemned by their own consciences. Jerome asks why men who would not put the money in the treasury shed the blood at all. Wesley is briefest: how easily could they digest innocent blood, and yet they had a conscience. Robertson hears in it the sentiment of Cain. Calvin observes that principals gain nothing by distinguishing themselves from their agents, the crime of one man acquitting nobody involved in it. Cyril of Jerusalem presses hardest, turning their words round: shall he who took and returned the price of murder see to it, and the murderers not see to it? and if the price is polluted, how is the deed not polluted too?

How he died is a genuine dispute. Lightfoot refuses the hanging outright and will not let the account in Acts be harmonised away: the devil who had lodged in him three days caught him up, strangled him, and flung him down so that he burst. Barnes and Clarke both keep the rope and break it, the fall accounting for what Acts records. Ellicott finds the Greek exact, the same word used of Ahithophel, suggesting only that a trembling hand may not have tied the noose firm. Where the money was thrown is disputed too: Gill puts it in the paved chamber where the council sat, Clarke by the temple door, Ellicott and Robertson inside the sanctuary itself, hurled past the veil.

The prophecy named is not where the name points, and the answers to that are six. Gill sets out exactly what Jeremiah does and does not contain. Jerome grants the quotation is from Zechariah and refuses to make it a falsehood, the Evangelist's business being the staple of doctrine and not words and syllables. Augustine canvasses everything: he rejects the copies reading only by the prophet, since the older ones name Jeremiah and nobody adds an error; he supposes the name rose in Matthew's memory and was left standing because the Spirit guiding that memory meant it to, which displays the consent of the prophets, who spoke by one Spirit so that each word belongs to all; and it is Jeremiah who buys a field and pays silver for it, so the reader is sent to compare the two. Lightfoot will have no error at all: Matthew wrote Jeremy and his countrymen understood it, the rabbis putting Jeremiah first in the order of the prophets. Barnes offers that explanation and two others, preferring a copyist's slip of one letter between the abbreviated names. Clarke reports the Hebrew apocryphal Jeremiah Jerome was shown, and thinks the words were put there to prop up this very quotation.
11:
The charge had to be changed before it could be used. Chrysostom says they knew Pilate cared nothing for the matters of their Law, so they turned to a charge of state, as they would afterwards do with the apostles, said to be proclaiming one Jesus king. Barnes puts it the same way: they had condemned him for blasphemy, knew a Roman governor would disregard that, and substituted treason. Robertson supplies the pressure on the other side, that Pilate could himself be accused to Caesar for disloyalty, rivals and pretenders being common across the empire. Henry notices the hypocrisy, a nation disaffected to Rome suddenly professing concern for Caesar's rights, and traces the charge to their own error, that whoever was the Christ must be a king who would break the Roman yoke.

The answer is short and much is made of its form. Origen has Pilate speaking not in doubt but affirmatively, as he would afterwards write it over the cross, so that the reply turns his own words into a confession. Hilary distinguishes the two formulas: to the high priest, who knew the Law and its promise of a Christ, the answer was thou hast said; to Pilate, who did not, it is thou sayest, because the salvation of the Gentiles hangs on that present confession. Chrysostom and Barnes agree that kingship was owned and at once qualified, the kingdom being not of this world, which Chrysostom supports from the reason that cannot be gainsaid, that the servants of an earthly king would have fought; and he recalls that Jesus had paid tribute and had fled when they wished to crown him. Ellicott judges that the explanation satisfied Pilate and accounts for his later efforts to release him.

The silence divides them. Jerome says the man who asked unwillingly got some answer while the chief priests were judged unworthy of a word, and adds that a defence might have persuaded the governor to release him, deferring the benefit of the cross. Origen makes Pilate unworthy too, a man with no settled opinion, veering between contradictory suppositions. Chrysostom splits the difference, holding that a little was said so that total silence should not be read as obstinacy. Clarke thinks no answer was needed, the accusations having refuted themselves. Calvin faces the objection that he was not wholly silent, and answers that a defence was at hand and voluntarily withheld: he was silent that he might now be our advocate, and his silence opens our mouth.

What astonished the governor is disputed. Barnes thinks it was the meekness rather than the want of a defence, since a defence was unnecessary but such bearing was unusual, and observes how little the charge could survive the sight of the accused, poor, unarmed, friendless and alone. Origen makes it wonder at endurance, a judge with power to condemn facing a prisoner of immovable gravity, so that it seemed a miracle that a man at a criminal bar should be unafraid of the death all men think terrible. Clarke reads the silence as magnanimity, which confounded the priests but affected Pilate, who had no interest in admiring it.

Two readers turn the trial round. Henry says he was arraigned that we might be discharged, and stood in that judgment that we might stand in God's. Calvin says the same at greater length: it is shocking that the Son of God should be dragged before a profane man and tried on a capital charge, but he was pronounced guilty on earth so that we might not be condemned in heaven; none are offended at it except the proud and those unashamed of their own iniquity. Augustine is occupied with the seam: Matthew here returns from the digression about the traitor, and it matters nothing to the truth in what order the evangelists relate events, or which omits what another gives.
15:
Chrysostom reads the custom as Pilate's second attempt at a rescue, devised so that the Jews should not be left the shadow of an excuse: if they would not have him go as innocent, they might at least yield him to the holy day as convicted. He notices that the transaction runs backwards. It is the populace who usually petition for a condemned man and the prince who grants; here the prince petitions the people, and by asking makes them more violent. Origen is colder, calling it the sort of favour conquerors show the subjected until the yoke is riveted, though he grants it had Jewish precedent, Saul having spared his son because all the people sought his life. Robertson notes that no parallel case has been found, only the historian's mention of it.

The prisoner's name carries a textual question. Clarke reports a Vatican manuscript with a marginal note that the oldest copies read the choice as between Jesus Barabbas and Jesus who is called Christ, and explains the usual omission by the scruple of Christian copyists, unwilling that a murderer should bear the Redeemer's name in the same verse. Ellicott weighs the same evidence as considerable though not decisive, points out that the name is a patronymic and wants a personal name beside it, and adds that since Abba was a title of honour for a Rabbi, the cry Jesus the Rabbi's son found more favour than Jesus the Nazarene. Jerome cites the Gospel according to the Hebrews, where the name is rendered son of their master. Lightfoot shows how ordinary the name was among the rabbis. Gill and Barnes agree that notable here means infamous.

Pilate's calculation is reconstructed the same way. Barnes thinks he counted on the popularity of Jesus against an odious robber, and that had the people been left to themselves it would have worked; he supposes the question was put in both forms, the Christ to move them and the King of the Jews to ridicule the priests. Ellicott calls it all but the last attempt to shift off the burden of responsibility. Robertson has him catching at straws, and observes that the two men set side by side were the leader of a revolt against Rome and a claimant to a spiritual kingdom, so that the governor unwittingly matched the antagonistic forces of all time.

That the motive was envy nobody doubts. Gill says he read it in their faces and their whole conduct, which had nothing to do with Caesar or justice. Ellicott names the thing precisely as fear of losing influence and power. Robertson adds that the envy was the leaders' and not the crowd's. Wesley says they envied him because the people magnified him. Clarke draws the conclusion the others leave: knowing that, it was the judge's plain business to disperse the mob and release the prisoner, and he remarks that malice springs from envy as often as from anger. Barnes states the same duty and then the difficulty, that had Pilate done it the Scriptures could not have been fulfilled; he leaves the tension standing and finds providence in it, that sentence came from a man satisfied of the prisoner's innocence.

Two readers take the scene somewhere else. Origen turns the exchange into a rule of the inner life: where Jesus is not there are strifes and fightings, and every man who does evil has Barabbas loosed in him and Jesus bound, while the man who does good has Christ loosed and Barabbas bound. Lightfoot recalls that at the siege of the city, when the Roman engines threw their stones, watchers on the towers warned the people in the common dialect with the cry that the Son was coming, which was the robber's own name; and he adds that the Son of man did indeed come then, in the glory of his justice.
19:
The dream is taken seriously by all and explained by none. Clarke states flatly that God had appeared to the woman, testifying the prisoner's innocence and warning what would follow if the blood were shed. Barnes is more cautious, allowing she may have been satisfied of his innocence by other means, and suggesting that her sleeping mind worked on what her waking mind already feared, judgment descending on her husband's house, dreams being treated as indications of the divine will by Romans and Greeks as well as Jews. Ellicott supplies what can be known of her: that governors under the Republic could not bring their wives to the provinces, a rule relaxed under the Empire, that an apocryphal Gospel names her Procula and calls her a proselyte, and that the second claim is likely enough, Jews at that period having gained influence over women of the higher classes. Lightfoot produces a rabbinic parallel for the very phrase, a king's mother sending word to have nothing to do with that Jew.

How the crowd was turned is described in detail. Gill thinks it was done not by public oratory but by servants sent among the people with two arguments, that the court had unanimously condemned a blasphemer, and that if he went free the Romans would take away their place and nation. Ellicott pictures the council before the palace mixing with the crowd, whispering now to one man and now another, praise of the robber and slander of the Christ. Robertson observes that Sadducees and Pharisees, who agreed on little, saw the peril together. Barnes notes that the release lay with the people and not the rulers, which is why the rulers had to work on the crowd at all. Calvin refuses to excuse the crowd and still insists on the distinction: they were not of their own accord hostile but sold themselves to gratify the priests, so that the death was demanded by the voice of the people, not because he was generally hated, but because most had enslaved their tongue to the conspiracy of a few.

That the same voices had lately said something else is the point both reach. Clarke sets the two cries side by side, the Son of David a few days since and a murderer preferred now, and draws the lesson against corrupt pastors, who can bring a flock to choose Barabbas over Jesus. Robertson makes it a remark about popular favour, the hero of the Sunday being the condemned criminal of the Friday.

The manner of death is named here for the first time, as Ellicott points out, and by the crowd rather than the priests: punish him as the robber and the rebel are punished. Wesley sees why the word came so readily, crucifixion being precisely what Barabbas had deserved; and he adds that in their malice they forgot what precedent they were handing a Roman governor, which within a few years turned dreadfully upon themselves. Calvin reports Pilate's last argument, an appeal not to pity but to shame: if you have no compassion for the man, have some regard for your own honour, since foreigners will conclude he was executed to chastise you all. Even that failed.

On the governor the verdicts converge and harden. Gill observes that of everything alleged not one criminal act had been proved. Barnes records that the question was put three times, that Pilate offered to scourge and release in hope of moving them, and calls him weak and irresolute, a man who should have preferred justice to popularity. Ellicott says the question attested his conviction and his cowardice together, the offer of a milder punishment only advertising his weakness and stiffening the crowd. Robertson is harshest: a feeble protest from a flickering conscience, a judge descending to argue with a mob, a scene closer to a lynching than a trial.
24:
The hand-washing is traced to a law and then dismissed as useless. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all point to the rite by which the elders of the city nearest an undiscovered murder washed their hands and disclaimed the blood. Robertson notes that the middle voice makes it a washing for himself, a claim of cleanliness with a slap at the crowd in it. Wesley records only that the custom was as much heathen as Jewish. Ellicott supposes the motive mixed, part relief of conscience, part deference to his wife, part a last dramatic appeal, and quotes a poet of Pilate's own time on the nullity of such ablutions: too easy souls, who think river water can lift the grim guilt of slaughter. Barnes and Clarke both answer the gesture the same way: a magistrate is bound to free an innocent man, Pilate had the armed force at his command and could have dispersed the mob, and could have cleared himself before the emperor had he been charged with sparing a seditious man. Calvin compares him to sailors who let a storm carry them out of their course, and refuses the excuse of necessity, since he ought rather to have suffered anything than swerve.

The imprecation is read two ways and the difference matters. Barnes and Clarke take the later history of the nation as its literal fulfilment, both noticing that when the city fell the Romans crucified so many that crosses ran short for the men and room for the crosses. Ellicott enters three cautions: only a fraction of the people stood there; some rulers, Joseph among them, had not consented; and the son does not bear the iniquity of the father except so far as he consents to it and reproduces it. Robertson is blunter still: Pilate's guilt was not washed off either, there was guilt enough to go round among Judas, Caiaphas, the council, the people and the governor, at bottom the sins of all of us nailed Jesus to the cross, and the words are no excuse for race hatred. Calvin draws a different moral, about men who will not take the trouble to distinguish right from wrong and are abandoned to a fury that ends in cursing themselves; and he observes that God nevertheless reserved a remnant.

Two readers make the release of Barabbas the shape of the whole transaction. Gill treats the robber as an emblem of those for whom Christ suffered, rebels and destroyers of themselves who are yet children of a Father, loosed when he was bound and acquitted when he was condemned. Henry puts the same thing as an inversion of a proverb: the common course of providence is that the wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and here the upright is a ransom for the transgressors.

On the scourging Lightfoot supplies the Roman practice, that those to be crucified were first beaten with whips before the judgment seat. Henry observes how little sense it made, since a man already sentenced had no need of rods, which were meant to supersede the axes rather than introduce them; and Roman scourging was not held within the forty stripes of the Jewish law. He turns it at the end: he was chastised with whips that we might not be for ever chastised with scorpions.

Calvin sets the scene at its widest. The supreme and sole Judge of the world is placed at the bar of an earthly judge, condemned as a malefactor, and set between two robbers as though he were the prince of robbers; a spectacle revolting enough to disturb the senses, until met by the argument that the punishment due to us was laid on him. He ends with the water, which did nothing for Pilate's stains and may still do something for ours, cleansing our eyes to see, in the midst of a condemnation, whose righteousness is on trial.
27:
The place and the numbers are settled first. Barnes and Clarke take the hall for the governor's own residence, the court having sat outside it because the Jews would not come in; Ellicott specifies the Tower of Antonia, whose portico faced the Temple court and whose barrack-room lay within. Barnes reckons that at a tenth of a legion, four to six hundred men.

The colour of the robe is a small harmonising problem. Augustine offers two solutions: a scarlet cloak used in mockery where royal purple was meant, one shade of purple being very like scarlet, or the other evangelist naming the purple the cloak contained though its colour was scarlet. Barnes gives the chemistry, scarlet from a fruit and purple from a shellfish, and observes that the ancients called any colour with red in it purple. Robertson traces the scarlet dye to the clustered insect that yields it. Ellicott identifies the garment itself, the military cloak worn by emperors in their character as generals. All assume it was cast off: Barnes cannot imagine Pilate lending a fresh robe for a mockery, Ellicott suggests a worn one of Pilate's or the one Herod had used, and Wesley says it was old and tattered.

Whether the crown was meant to hurt is a real dispute. Clarke says it was not an instrument of torture but of ridicule, like the reed and the bent knee, argues the plant was probably acanthus rather than thorn in our sense, and complains that Christians have gone astray in magnifying the sufferings from this one circumstance, painters being the worst commentators of all. Barnes takes the other side: the shrub was one with sharp points of hard wood, easily pressed into the skin, so that the mockery increased the pain. Gill will not decide what plant it was and thinks it hardly matters.

The fathers read every article of the costume. Jerome takes the scarlet for the bloody works of the Gentiles, the crown for the ancient curse taken away, and the reed as the instrument with which the sacrilege of the Jews was written down. Hilary makes the scarlet the blood of all the martyrs, finds in the thorns the sins of the Gentiles that once pierced him, and says the crown of victory is woven from the prick in them; the reed is the frailty of the Gentiles he takes into his hand, his head struck with it so that their weakness may rest on the Father, who is his head. Origen makes the reed the broken staff of Egypt on which men leaned before they believed, taken up now to be triumphed over by the wood of the cross. Remigius keeps closer to the surface: the scarlet is the Lord's flesh reddened by his own blood, the crown his bearing our sins in the likeness of sinful flesh. Augustine alone turns the changed clothing into an argument: stripping his own garment and putting on another answers the heretics who said his body was a shadow.

Chrysostom counts the indignities rather than interpreting them. Not one member but the whole body was made an object of insolence: the head by the crown and the reed and the buffeting, the face by the spitting, the cheeks by the palms, the whole body by the stripes and the robe and the pretended worship, the hand by the reed given it for a sceptre. He asks what plea we can have for resenting an injury after this, and observes that the soldiers had not even the Jews' envy to plead, but made a pleasure of cruelty. Lightfoot recalls a rabbinic tale of an angel in Solomon's shape holding a reed and struck with a reed. Clarke ends with the moral he found in an older writer, that Christ in this condition preaches to the kings of the earth that their sceptres are only reeds.
32:
Why this man out of the crowd is a question only Ellicott presses. He notes the Jewish settlement at Cyrene and that the other evangelist names Simon as father of Alexander and Rufus, later known in the Church; from which he infers that Simon may already have been suspected of discipleship, and was seized for that reason. Robertson explains the verb instead, a Persian word for impressing a courier into service, denying that the soldiers meant a jest on Simon. Clarke thinks the cross was carried part of the way by Christ himself and that Simon was made to assist rather than to take it entirely, and quotes the moralist who used the custom to illustrate vice, every wickedness bringing its own torment as every malefactor carries his own cross.

That the impressment argues bodily failure they all see. Robertson lists what had gone before, Gethsemane, the betrayal, a sleepless night and the scourging, and adds the weight of the world's sin. Calvin makes the same point by comparison: the men usually crucified were robbers of great bodily strength who could bear such a burden, and the weakness that could not showed plainly that it was a lamb being sacrificed. He adds that the punishment was so detestable a man thought himself polluted if he so much as put a hand to the wood, which is why they seized a peasant; and he notices that the evangelists record not only the name but the country and children of a man taken from the lowest dregs, as though God meant to ennoble him by his heralds.

On the place there is a spelling question and a moral. Gill and Lightfoot both observe that the form should strictly be Golgoltha, the dropped letter being ordinary in Syriac, and Lightfoot defends the text against a critic who thought it corrupt. Henry supposes it the common place of execution and perhaps the charnel-house where skulls were laid out of the way, and finds the fitness of it: here lay the trophies of death's victory, and Christ in destroying death triumphed over it on its own ground.

The drink raises a harmonising problem, since one evangelist gives vinegar and gall and another wine and myrrh. Barnes dissolves it by vocabulary: vinegar was thin wine gone sour and the common drink of the soldiers, so either word would serve, myrrh and gall alike meaning anything exceedingly bitter. Lightfoot divides it differently, taking the one account for the national custom and the other for what was actually done, so that a cup was indeed given as custom required, but not the customary mixture. Clarke sets out the conjecture that the difficulty is a translator's, an original Aramaic phrase for sweet wine with bitters having been read as vinegar and gall; he reports a rival reconstruction and is not satisfied with either.

Whether the cup was mercy or malice divides them sharply. Lightfoot says it was prepared not by the women who out of compassion paid for such drinks but by the persecutors, who studied to heap on every kind of vexation. Clarke says the opposite, that someone appears to have offered it out of kindness. Barnes stands between, recording only that the draught was commonly given to deaden the pains of crucifixion. On the refusal they converge. Barnes has him unwilling to blunt the pains of dying, choosing instead the cup his Father gave. Clarke has him determined to endure the fullness of pain and to tread the winepress alone. Henry makes the finest distinction of the three: he tasted it and would not drink it, taking the bitterness into his mouth because he would let no bitter cup pass untasted while he was atoning for our tasting of forbidden fruit, but refusing the opiate because he had work to do as a priest in his suffering and meant to feel himself die.
35:
The evangelist says only that they crucified him, and Gill supplies what the words cover: the cross laid flat, the arms drawn out and nailed, the feet fixed on a basis in the upright, the whole raised and left standing until the man on it died. Augustine takes the horror as the point: it belongs to living rightly not to fear what should not be feared, and though many who do not fear death dread some particular death, none was more fearful than this, which is why it was chosen to teach that none is to be dreaded. He then runs through the history of wood: the ark that carried the race through the flood, the rod that divided the sea, the wood cast into the bitter water that made it sweet, the rod that drew the stream from the rock, the staff that held up the hands by which Amalech was beaten, so that by these steps we come at last to the wood of the cross, where Adam recovered what he lost at a tree. The Gloss adds only that the four arms answer to the four quarters of the earth.

Chrysostom notices two things nobody else does. He was lifted up in the open air and not under a roof, so that the air itself might be purified and the earth cleansed by what fell from him; and the stripping was a particular contempt, the garments of the condemned being divided only when a man was too poor to leave anything else, which they did not do for the robbers. Robertson sees the incongruity, rough men casting lots for clothes, a comedy at the foot of the tragedy of the ages. Jerome finds the guard useful in the end, the vigilance of soldiers and priests making the power of the resurrection harder to deny.

The title is read as accusation and proclamation at once. Jerome cannot get over the enormity: after buying false witnesses and raising a riot they could find nothing to put on the board except that he was King of the Jews, and even that perhaps in mockery. Remigius takes it as providence, so that the Jews might learn that killing him would not rid them of their King, his sovereignty being confirmed by the very instrument of his death. Origen sets it beside the plate on the high priest's forehead inscribed Holiness to the Lord, the true High Priest carrying his title on the cross. Clarke describes the custom of the placard and recalls that the priests asked for the wording to be altered and were refused. Barnes and Ellicott both face the four different forms the evangelists give and settle it the same way, by the three languages: the inscription need not have run identically in each.

The robbers are made to mean a great deal. Calvin keeps to the shame: he was not set apart from them, which might have marked a distinction, but raised in the middle as though he were the prince of robbers, the finishing stroke of disgrace, required so that he might stand in our room. Hilary sees the whole race called to the Passion and divided by it, believers on the right and unbelievers on the left, the one saved by the justification of faith. Leo reads the same figure as the separation to be made at the judgment, the instrument provided for a punishment being made by the Redeemer into a step towards glory.

The historians ask who the two were. Lightfoot fills in the word from the records of the period, the bands that burnt the palaces at Jericho, the daggermen who killed in daylight in the city. Ellicott and Robertson both think the two belonged to Barabbas's band, since no trial of theirs is recorded; Barnes adds that the middle cross was the one Barabbas should have filled.
39:
The taunt offers a bargain and the readers refuse it on his behalf. Chrysostom turns the condition inside out: he does not come down from the cross precisely because he is the Son of God, having come for no other purpose than to be crucified. Jerome answers the promise of belief by comparing the miracles, since rising from a tomb is the greater and they did not believe that either; and he adds that the demons, already feeling their strength broken, put the words into men's mouths to get him off the wood, so that he stayed on it to destroy the Devil. Pseudo-Chrysostom hears whose voice it is, the father of these children having said once before, if thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down. Leo turns on the mockers: what teacher had told them the true King of Israel would be one who refused to be crucified? Not the prophets, who spoke of a face not hidden from spitting, of pierced hands and feet, and of a Lord who reigned from the tree.

The second taunt concedes more than it means to. Gill takes the words less as admission than insinuation, the cures and raisings being illusions or done by the Devil's help. Barnes agrees it is cutting irony rather than concession, and explains the silence: the time for the atonement had come, proof enough had been given, and the people would have been no better satisfied had he stepped down. Ellicott makes the finer point that the mockers bear unconscious witness to the truth, as an earlier speaker in that council had done. Clarke sets the offence and the answer side by side: a high priest who would destroy the temple, a Saviour who cannot save himself and a crucified Son of God are the contradictions that give offence; rightly read, they are a high priest opening a heavenly sanctuary, a Saviour dying as the victim of salvation, and a Son of God confining his power within the bounds of the cross.

The third taunt quotes Scripture without knowing it. Ellicott finds it barely conceivable that priests and scribes should recite the very words of a psalm and so fulfil the prophecy, and explains it twice: they did not read that psalm as Messianic, and familiarity would bring its phrases to the lips when the occasion called for them. Robertson notes that they added a word the psalm does not have, the impatient now. Calvin takes the taunt as Satan's sharpest arrow, the argument that God does not love those he does not immediately assist; nothing is less reasonable, he answers, than to limit God's love to a point of time, and delay is often the testimony of a father.

That the robbers reviled him too sets a harmonising problem, since the other evangelist gives one of them repenting, and the solutions are six. Chrysostom says both reviled at first and not afterwards, using the fact as proof against collusion: the penitent was a real robber and a real enemy first, and was changed. Jerome offers the same sequence with a cause, the withdrawn sun and the shaken earth working the change, or else reads the pair as the two nations. Augustine and Calvin both call it a figure of speech, the plural standing for the singular, Calvin adding that they meant only to show him attacked on every hand, down to the class of dying criminals. Gill defends the idiom from the Hebrew, where a man goes down into the sides of a ship. Barnes offers both explanations without choosing. Robertson reads the imperfect as inchoative and the sense as even the robbers, who for a moment felt themselves above him. Hilary alone declines to soften it, taking the fact that both cast his Passion in his teeth as a sign that the cross was bound to offend everyone, the faithful included.
45:
Origen states the objection before answering it. An eclipse falls when the moon passes beneath the sun, which cannot happen at the Passover, when the moon is full; and unbelievers press the further point that no Greek or foreign observer recorded it, one chronicler having noted such an event under Tiberius without saying it fell at the full moon. He will not take refuge in the answer that the laws of nature were simply suspended. His own solution is that the darkness, like the torn veil and the earthquake, was local, covering Jerusalem or at most Judaea for three hours. Chrysostom answers from duration rather than extent, an eclipse being transient where this lasted three hours; and he insists on the opposite geography, the wonder lying in its covering the whole earth, as had happened only once before, in Egypt at the Passover, which was the type of this.

Why nobody was converted by it Chrysostom also asks. The hour was chosen at midday so that every dweller on earth should see it; it was the sign of Jonas promised to the generation that demanded one; and it came after the mockery was spent. His answer is that the age was sunk in sluggishness, the wonder single and soon over, and nobody troubled to look for its cause, some no doubt setting it down to an eclipse after all.

Origen prefers to read the hours, Egypt having three days of darkness and Judaea three, and the light returning at the ninth as a promise that when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel shall be saved. Pseudo-Chrysostom keeps to the outrage itself: the creation could not bear what was done to the Creator, so the sun withdrew his beams rather than look on it, the source of living water being made to drink vinegar.

The cry divides them more sharply than the darkness. Origen rejects the easy answer that it was said out of humility, and asks the reader to measure the glory he had against the shame he accepted; he warns against taking the words after the manner of men, as though misery had wrung them out, since the loud voice points to something greater hidden in them. Hilary reports the use heretics made of the verse, that the Word was absorbed into the soul, or that an ordinary man was left to die when the divine support was withdrawn. Clarke meets the same error head on and refuses the suggestion that the deity departed at that hour: take deity away from any redeeming act, he says, and redemption is ruined. Barnes builds his answer in layers: the bodily anguish, the permitted return of the tempter in what was called the power of darkness, the withholding of consolations that have carried martyrs cheerfully to the stake, and beneath all something deeper, a manifestation to his soul of God's hatred of sin, endured in our place.

The words themselves are a small philological problem. Barnes calls the language neither Hebrew nor Syriac but a mixture, probably what he ordinarily spoke; Clarke says that as the evangelists give it, it is neither. Jerome notes that a clause in the middle of the verse is superfluous to the Hebrew, and holds it impious to read the psalm of David or Esther when the evangelist has applied its clauses to the Saviour. On the bystanders he offers two explanations: Roman soldiers who caught only the first word, or Jews pretending to hear an appeal to Elias so as to charge him with weakness. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic parallel in which Esther uses the same ejaculation, and reads the hour as the one when the chain was slackened and the whole malice of hell was let loose at a single stroke. Gill notices what else was happening at the ninth hour, the slaying of the daily sacrifice.
50:
Henry makes the loud cry the evidence. The voice is among the first things to fail in dying men; this man spoke at the last like one in full strength, which shows that the life was not taken from him but delivered up, and that he who could cry out so could have loosed himself from arrest. He hears in it a shout of mastery over the powers he was spoiling, and calls it a trumpet blown over the sacrifice; and he notes that the hour was that of the evening sacrifice and the killing of the paschal lamb.

On the veil, Origen supposes two, the outer rent so that mysteries hidden with good reason until the Lord's coming might now be published, the inner waiting for a later unveiling, when what is perfect is come and the true ark may be seen as it is. Hilary reads it as dispossession, the nation dispersed and the honour of the veil withdrawn along with the angel who had guarded it. Lightfoot makes a physical objection the others miss: the tearing of a hanging can hardly be laid to the earthquake, a shock breaking hard things rather than soft and rending rocks sooner than curtains, so the curtain was a separate miracle. Clarke, attributing the opened graves to the earthquake without hesitation, takes the opposite view of what a tremor could do.

Augustine attends to the seams. The words and behold fix the rending at the moment of death rather than leaving it a displaced recollection, so the three accounts can stand in their own order. He shows that the centurion feared at the earthquake and wondered at the loud death without contradiction, the death being among the things that were done. And he offers two ways of reconciling the women who stood far off with those who stood near: a distance near enough to be in his sight and far only by comparison with the crowd at the foot, or a withdrawal after the mother was committed to the disciple.

The risen saints are the hardest thing here, and are handled with unusual care. Jerome lays down the rule the others follow: the graves were opened at the death, but nobody rose before the Lord, that he might keep the primacy of the resurrection. Barnes agrees, and thinks them lately dead, since saints of an older generation would not have been recognised or believed. Ellicott states the difficulties without flinching: the passage stands alone in the New Testament and has been called a myth, or explained as bodies merely exposed by the shock, or as an honest report of an overheated imagination. Against all of which he sets the bareness of the telling, legend being given to luxuriant expansion. He connects it with the apostle's language about a preaching to the spirits in prison, and departs from tradition by refusing to identify the risen with the patriarchs of an apocryphal gospel: the men came out of graves in Jerusalem, and the word saints was used from the first of disciples.

The allegorists take the same signs inward. Origen makes the shaken earth all flesh, the rent rocks the depths of the prophets opened, and the graves the bodies of souls dead to God, which become bodies of saints when grace raises them and they walk out of themselves in newness of life. Hilary is briefer and bolder: the earth quaked because unequal to contain such a body, the rocks were rent because the Word that pierces all strong things had gone through them, and the graves opened because the bands of death were loosed. Leo turns it into exhortation: the rocks of unbelieving minds should be rent and those shut up in the sepulchres of mortality should burst their bonds, so that what we believe of the body may happen in the heart.
54:
What the centurion meant is read at three different heights. Lightfoot takes the confession at full value: the words mean that this was indeed the Messiah, a title the Jews themselves gave to the Messiah as a son by adoption and deputation, the officer having picked up the expectation by living among them and applied it on the evidence of what he had seen. Barnes and Clarke take it low. Barnes points out that the Greek is a son of a god, a form suited to a polytheist, and supposes the man had no distinct notion beyond the deified heroes of his own religion, though he took the wonders for proof that the prisoner was what he claimed. Clarke says the same more briefly, that in Roman usage the phrase would mean an eminent or divine person and nothing more. Ellicott settles between them by insisting that the words be interpreted from the centurion's knowledge and not from Christian faith: what they would carry to him is one God-like in righteousness and holiness and love, the form of words being supplied by the taunt he had heard thrown about all afternoon.

That another evangelist reports him saying instead that this was a righteous man is handled three ways. Lightfoot supposes both sentences were spoken, one after the other. Barnes thinks the sayings came from different men in the guard or at different moments. Ellicott treats the other report as a softening of the same witness, and holds that what Matthew gives probably meant little more than what Luke gives.

On the women the commentators speak with one voice, and the voice is sharp. Gill asks where Peter was, who had said he would never be offended, and the rest who said the same, and answers that none was present but one, while many women of the weaker sex stood there, which rebuked at once the earlier boasting and the present cowardice. Clarke says they showed more courage and attachment than the men who had promised to die with him. Barnes supposes they were kept back by the soldiers rather than by choice, and that while multitudes of men joined the cry and deserted him, not one of the women who followed him is recorded as unfaithful. Calvin puts it as providence rather than praise: when the disciples were scattered the Lord retained some of their company as witnesses; and although the one disciple did not leave the cross, no mention is made of him here, the commendation falling on the women alone, whose attachment showed the more plainly because the men were trembling.

Robertson gives the group its epitaph: these were the women last at the cross and first at the tomb, the mother having by then been taken home by the disciple to whom she was committed. He names the three and refuses to guess at their anguish, dropping the curtain with a question: what hope did life hold for them now?

Who they were is less easily settled. On the surname they offer three derivations: the town on the lake, a word meaning a plaiter of women's hair, and the Hebrew for a tower, taken to signify the strength of her faith. Gill and Clarke both report the second, and Lightfoot fills it out with rabbinic material about a woman of that trade. On identity there is a flat disagreement. Lightfoot follows an earlier scholar in holding Magdalene to be the sister of Lazarus, arguing from this very passage, since otherwise that sister was either absent from the crucifixion or passed over in silence, both improbable. Clarke reports the same opinion while himself distinguishing four Marys in the Gospels. Robertson rejects the identification outright, and with it the other common conflation, holding that she is neither the sinful woman of the earlier chapter nor the sister of Lazarus at all.
57:
Why the evangelist mentions the man's wealth Jerome answers at once: not to boast a noble disciple, but to explain how he could get the body at all, since poor and unknown men would not have dared approach Roman power to ask for a crucified malefactor. Chrysostom admires the courage rather than the standing: a man risking his life and taking on many enmities, daring not only to ask for the body but to bury it. Henry makes the same point about the money: worldly wealth is to many an obstacle in religion's way, yet in some services it is an advantage, and well for those who have it if they have also a heart to use it; and he adds that Christ has more secret disciples than we know of. Gill notes that the man went in boldly, unashamed of a crucified Christ. Ellicott finds Pilate's ready compliance of a piece with his earlier behaviour, a lingering reverence that helps the friends rather than the foes of the sufferer.

Lightfoot explains the alternative. The law forbade leaving a body on the tree overnight, and those executed by the council were buried not with their fathers but in one of two appointed grounds, the disgrace being reckoned to make some atonement. It was to spare him that burial that Joseph asked, and the council, had they been consulted, would not readily have allowed it.

Almost everything else is read as a safeguard against fraud, ancient and modern readers agreeing closely. Jerome gives three: a new tomb, lest it be said that some other body there had risen; a tomb cut in rock, lest it be said the foundations were undermined; and a great stone, which no one could roll back without the strength of many. Pseudo-Augustine reduces it to two objections foreclosed: that they dug through the ground, and that they carried him off while the guard slept. Barnes repeats the list and adds one of his own, that the untenanted tomb answers the suggestion that he was revived by contact with a prophet's bones, as had happened once before. Clarke turns it around: had he been buried in the common ground of executed men, no one would have sealed a stone or set a watch, so that the very precautions of his enemies furnished the evidence.

The same circumstance is also read as prophecy. Barnes and Clarke both find the grave made with the rich where the life had been passed among the poor, and Clarke draws a line through it: while still the sacrifice he was numbered with transgressors, but the atonement once made he is no longer enrolled with them. Calvin credits none of it to design, holding that the untouched sepulchre came about by secret providence rather than premeditation, to distinguish him from the rest of the race and mark his newness of life.

The cloth attracts attention on its own account. Barnes and Clarke explain that the spices were folded into the wrappings for want of time to embalm properly, which is why the women came back with more. Remigius reads the cloth instead, grown out of the earth and brought to whiteness by great labour, as the body taken from earth and brought through the passion to the whiteness of immortality. Hilary makes Joseph a figure of the apostles and the linen the sheet let down from heaven, so that the Church is buried with Christ; the rock-hewn chamber is the hard breast of the Gentiles, cut open by the labour of teaching, and the stone is rolled to the mouth because after him no other author of divine knowledge is to be admitted. Remigius ends with the women, who marked the place with anxious care so that at a fit time they might do their office, as the lowly souls of the saints still wait while the passion is completed.
62:
That the precautions defeated themselves is what everybody sees. Chrysostom states it most fully: the sealing testifies that he had died and been buried, and if the tomb was watched no fraud was possible, so that an empty tomb afterwards proves the resurrection. He adds a detail the rest miss, that Pilate would not let the soldiers seal it alone but made the priests do it themselves, so that they could not afterwards accuse the guard of letting the body go. Hilary calls it folly and unbelief, sealing the tomb of one at whose word they had watched a dead man walk out of another. Clarke separates the two measures: the guard was to stop the disciples stealing the body, the seal to stop the guard being bribed. Barnes lists the circumstances: the enemies judged him dead, had their own way about the burial, chose the place and the number of the watch, and so furnished the proof. Calvin puts it shortest, that with Pilate's signet they shut their own mouths as surely as they shut the sepulchre.

Chrysostom notices something else, that the evangelists conceal none of the opprobrious language, the word deceiver included, which shows both the savagery of the accusers, who could not let their anger go even after the death, and the truthfulness of the men who wrote it down. Cyril of Jerusalem answers the charge itself: the cross was no illusion and the death no mere show, since otherwise the redemption would be an illusion too.

How they came to remember the saying is disputed. Ellicott draws a sharp inference: they had stirred the people by taking the words about the temple literally, yet had understood the real meaning themselves, seeing further here than the disciples did, because sorrow confuses while suspicion sharpens. Robertson meets the objection that the rulers could not have known of such a prediction by pointing out that it was made to them expressly, and names the critic who dismissed the story as unhistorical. Clarke sees them refuting themselves: they had killed him for the words about the temple taken one way, and now declare the other meaning, and so are taken in their own craftiness.

Remigius takes up the arithmetic of the three days and rejects the expedient of counting the three hours of darkness as a night and the returning light as a day, on the ground that they do not know the force of figurative speech. His own reckoning runs from the day of the crucifixion with its preceding night, through the night and day of the sabbath, to the night and day of the Lord's own. Augustine leaves the counting alone and reads the number, the three days answering to the consent of the whole Trinity in the passion, the Three who made man in the beginning restoring him at the end. Jerome only remarks that crucifying him had not been enough: they must guard the grave as well.

The governor's reply is a small grammatical question. Ellicott and Gill both read it as a command, take ye a guard, for the same reason: had the priests had a guard of their own, they would have had no occasion to ask. Barnes takes the other reading and supposes the band appointed for the crucifixion was still at their service, since the dying could last for days. Clarke thinks of the companies then off duty, Wesley of the garrison in the tower. Robertson hears the tone rather than the mood, a curt permission thrown to men the speaker despised. Barnes alone asks how a stone was sealed, and offers cords brought together and closed with wax under a signet, as a king's den of lions had once been sealed. Gill ends with an irony: if the tomb lay further off than a sabbath day's journey, they broke their own tradition to secure it.
